parts.t: Chilliwack land use plans, OCP maps, and zoning updates help buyers, sellers, and investors understand where future growth, redevelopment, and new housing opportunities are happening across Sardis, Downtown Chilliwack, Promontory, Fairfield Island, and surrounding neighbourhoods. These official community plans provide guidance on density, land use, infrastructure, and long-term development, making them essential for tracking property values and investment potential throughout the city.

lines.text: The Sardis Neighbourhood is centrally located in Chilliwack, immediately south of Highway 1, and is bordered by the ALR (west and east), First Nations Lands (south and east), and the Vedder neighbourhood to the south. The Plan sets out planning principles and associated policies to guide decisions on land use and development in the neighbourhood. It is a tool kit for City staff, Council, industry, and residents alike.

The Chilliwack Downtown Land Use and Development Plan articulates the community’s vision for the Downtown Plan Area over the next 30 years. Founded on a strong based of community engagement, the Plan gives clear direction with regards to land use, housing, commercial and economic vitality, public open spaces, community facilities and programs, transportation, infrastructure, and the form and character of public and private realm development.
Chilliwack Proper and Fairfield Island Plan

The Chilliwack Proper and Fairfield Island Neighbourhoods have been divided into four distinct planning areas and surround the downtown: Mountainview (east of downtown), Riverside (north of downtown), Townsend (west of downtown) and Fairfield Island. These areas are expected to accommodate moderate densification in the form of smaller lot single family detached housing, duplexes, coach houses or garden suites, rowhouses, and, in select locations, townhouses and low rise apartments.

The Promontory Development Plan was completed in 1994. The primary purpose of the Promontory Development Plan is to facilitate the building of a viable, all inclusive community in Promontory. Although it was not formally adopted as part of the OCP, it was endorsed by Council and has guided the development of Promontory ever since.

The Alder area is currently undergoing a transformation towards a more mixed-use, apartment oriented sub-area in accordance with the Alder Neighbourhood Plan adopted by Council in 2014, following a comprehensive planning process. Located adjacent to a portion of the Valley Rail Trail Corridor and its proximity to Vedder Road, the Alder Area is a prime location to continue to support increased density and redevelopment.

The South Vedder Neighbourhood is a component of the broader Vedder Neighbourhood in the south end of the City of Chilliwack. As identified in its namesake, the South Vedder Neighbourhood is located in the southern portion of Vedder and borders the Chilliwack/Vedder River (south), and Promontory Neighbourhood (south-east), Tzeachten First Nations Lands (east), and the broader Vedder Neighbourhood (north and west). Vedder Road forms the western boundary of the South Vedder Neighbourhood.

blocks.text: Chilliwack Land Use Plans & 2050 OCP Real Estate FAQs

parts.t: What is the difference between Chilliwack's Official Community Plan (OCP) and Zoning Bylaw?

Zoning Bylaw 2020, No. 5000 sets the current legal rules for a parcel (permitted uses, building setbacks, height, lot coverage, and minimum lot size for subdivision today). The Chilliwack 2050 Official Community Plan (Bylaw No. 5500) sets long-term policy showing what higher density or land use City Council supports if an owner applies to rezone.
Where does the Sardis Neighbourhood Plan allow townhomes and infill density?

The Sardis Neighbourhood Plan (OCP Schedule D) concentrates medium- and high-density residential and mixed-use growth along the Vedder Road corridor, around Luckakuck Way and Promontory Road, and transitions into low-density residential infill (such as R1-B/R1-C small lots and duplexes) on surrounding interior streets.
How does BC's Small-Scale Multi-Unit Housing (SSMUH) legislation apply in Chilliwack?

Following provincial SSMUH rules and Chilliwack's zoning updates, eligible single-family urban lots inside the Urban Growth Boundary and serviced by municipal water and sewer can accommodate secondary suites, accessory dwelling units (coach houses), or multi-unit infill subject to zoning setbacks, parking, and floodplain rules.
What is Development Permit Area 2 (DPA2) in Chilliwack?

DPA2 is Chilliwack's Hillside and Upland Development Permit Area covering sloped neighbourhoods such as Promontory, Chilliwack Mountain, Little Mountain, Eastern Hillsides, Ryder Lake, Majuba Hill, and Vedder Mountain. It requires geotechnical, stormwater, and wildfire-interface engineering before subdivision, land clearing, or building.
How do Chilliwack's Fraser River and Vedder Alluvial Fan floodplain rules affect building?

Under Floodplain Regulation Bylaw No. 4519, new habitable floor space in designated floodplains must be built at or above the specified Flood Construction Level (FCL) and set back from dikes and watercourses, which often affects whether an in-ground basement is permitted on valley-floor lots.
Can Agricultural Land Reserve (ALR) parcels in Chilliwack be subdivided for housing?

Approximately 67% of Chilliwack is in the ALR, where both the Agricultural Land Commission (ALC) and the City's Agricultural Area Plan restrict subdivision and non-farm uses to preserve contiguous farmland. Subdivision inside the ALR requires ALC approval and is rarely granted for residential development.
How can I check the OCP designation and zoning on a specific Chilliwack address?

You can look up any Chilliwack parcel on the City of Chilliwack Webmap (checking Zoning, OCP Land Use, DPA overlays, and Floodplain layers) or send the address to Jared Gibbons at 604-928-1361 or jaredgibbons@royallepage.ca for a complimentary zoning and infill review.
